questions.question: What is inheritance in Java and how do you implement it?
questions.title: Inheritance in Java with extends Keyword
questions.direct_answer: **Inheritance** lets a **child (sub) class** acquire the fields and methods of a **parent (super) class** using the `extends` keyword, then add or override behavior. It models an **IS-A** relationship (`Dog extends Animal` — a dog *is an* animal) and promotes **code reuse**. Java supports single, multilevel, and hierarchical inheritance — but **not** multiple inheritance through classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement inheritance with extends and know it's an IS-A relationship aimed at reuse and polymorphism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using inheritance just to reuse code when the IS-A relationship doesn't truly hold.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Run the IS-A test before using extends, mention @Override and super, and note Java has no multiple inheritance of classes.

sections.title: Inheritance in Java — Quick Overview
sections.content:
**Inheritance** is the mechanism by which one class (the **child** or **subclass**) acquires the members of another (the **parent** or **superclass**) using `extends`. The child gets the parent's accessible fields and methods, can add its own, and can **override** inherited behavior.

It models an **IS-A** relationship: `Dog extends Animal` says a dog *is an* animal. The benefits are **code reuse** (shared behavior lives once in the parent) and **polymorphism** (treat a `Dog` as an `Animal`).

Java supports single, multilevel (`A → B → C`), and hierarchical (`B, C → A`) inheritance — but a class can `extends` only **one** parent.

sections.content:
amber|What it is|~child acquires parent|extends keyword|gets fields + methods|add or override
blue|IS-A test|~use before extends|Dog IS-A Animal|run it first|fails -> use composition
emerald|Benefits|~why use it|code reuse|polymorphism|shared base behavior
violet|Java's rule|~one parent only|single, multilevel, hierarchical|NO multiple via classes|use interfaces instead

sections.title: Implementing Inheritance
Inheritance misused — IS-A fails
Use inheritance only when IS-A holds
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inheriting only for reuse**: if `Child` is not truly a `Parent`, use composition instead.
- **Forgetting `super(...)`**: a subclass constructor must initialize the parent (implicit `super()` if you omit it).
- **Skipping `@Override`**: without it, a signature typo silently creates a new method instead of overriding.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `extends` gives a subclass the parent's fields and methods, plus its own.
- Models **IS-A**; aimed at **code reuse** and **polymorphism**.
- Run the **IS-A test** before using inheritance.
- Java: single, multilevel, hierarchical — **no multiple inheritance of classes**.
- Use `@Override` and `super` correctly; prefer composition when IS-A fails.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Inheritance is the mechanism that lets one class acquire the fields and methods of another. The class that inherits is the child or subclass, and the one it inherits from is the parent or superclass, and you connect them with the extends keyword. The child gets everything accessible from the parent, can add its own members, and can override inherited methods to specialize behavior. The relationship inheritance models is IS-A. Dog extends Animal means a dog is an animal. That's the test I always run before I use it: is the child genuinely a kind of the parent? If yes, inheritance fits. The two big benefits are code reuse and polymorphism. Code reuse, because shared behavior like an eat method lives once in the Animal parent and every subclass gets it for free. Polymorphism, because I can treat a Dog as an Animal — an Animal reference can point to a Dog object, and calling sound dispatches to the Dog's version. To implement it, the subclass constructor calls super to initialize the parent part of the object, and I put the Override annotation on any method I'm overriding so the compiler verifies I matched the signature. Java supports a few forms: single inheritance, multilevel where A extends B extends C, and hierarchical where several classes extend one parent. But a class can only extend one parent — there's no multiple inheritance through classes, because of the diamond problem; for that you use interfaces. The main mistake to avoid is reaching for inheritance purely to reuse some methods when the IS-A relationship doesn't actually hold. If the child isn't truly a kind of the parent, you should use composition instead — hold the other object and delegate to it.

questions.question: How do you use super to access parent class members in Java?
questions.title: Using super to Access Parent Members in Java
questions.direct_answer: `super` is a reference to the **parent class part** of the current object. Use **`super.method()`** to call the parent's version of an overridden method, **`super.field`** to access a hidden parent field, and **`super(args)`** as the first statement of a constructor to invoke the parent's constructor. It lets a subclass extend, rather than fully replace, inherited behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know super's three uses and that super(...) must be the first statement of a constructor.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting super(...) must be first, or not realizing super.method() is how you reuse the parent's overridden implementation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show super.method() lets an override augment the parent's behavior (e.g. call super.save() then add logging) instead of duplicating it.

sections.title: Using super — Quick Overview
sections.content:
`super` refers to the **parent class portion** of the current object. It has three uses:

1. **`super(args)`** — calls the parent's **constructor**; must be the **first statement** in a subclass constructor (an implicit `super()` is inserted if you omit it).
2. **`super.method()`** — calls the **parent's version** of a method you've overridden, so your override can build on it instead of replacing it.
3. **`super.field`** — accesses a parent field that the subclass has **hidden** with a same-named field.

The most useful in practice is `super.method()`: it lets you *extend* inherited behavior — do the parent's work, then add yours.

sections.title: Three Uses of super
sections.content:
amber|super(args)|~call parent constructor|first statement only|initializes parent part|implicit super() if omitted
blue|super.method()|~call parent's overridden method|reuse parent behavior|then add your own|augment, not replace
emerald|super.field|~access hidden parent field|when names collide|rarely needed|avoid field hiding
violet|Meaning|~parent part of this object|not a separate object|same instance|extends, not replaces

sections.title: All Three Uses of super
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`super(...)` not first**: it must be the first statement of the constructor, or it's a compile error.
- **Duplicating parent logic**: copy-pasting instead of calling `super.method()` then extending.
- **Relying on field hiding**: same-named fields are confusing — prefer not to hide fields at all.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `super` = the **parent part** of the current object (same instance).
- `super(args)` calls the parent constructor — **first statement** only.
- `super.method()` calls the parent's overridden method to **build on** it.
- `super.field` reaches a hidden parent field (avoid hiding when possible).
- Use `super.method()` to **augment** inherited behavior, not duplicate it.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The super keyword is a reference to the parent class portion of the current object, and it has three main uses. The first is super with arguments, which calls the parent's constructor. This has to be the very first statement in a subclass constructor, and its job is to initialize the parent part of the object before the subclass adds its own. If you don't write it, the compiler inserts an implicit call to the parent's no-arg constructor for you. The second use, and honestly the most useful day to day, is super dot method. When you've overridden a method, calling super dot that method runs the parent's original version. That lets your override build on top of the parent's behavior instead of throwing it away. A classic example is overriding a save method: you call super dot save to do the parent's actual saving, and then you add a log line afterward. You get to augment the behavior rather than duplicate it. The third use is super dot field, which accesses a field in the parent when the subclass has declared a field with the same name and hidden it. That one's rare, and honestly field hiding is something I'd avoid because it's confusing — two fields with the same name in a hierarchy is a recipe for bugs. The key mental model is that super isn't pointing at a separate object; it's the same object, just letting you reach the parent's version of things. The most common mistake is forgetting that super with arguments must come first in the constructor — you can't run any code before it, or it won't compile.

questions.question: Why does Java not support multiple inheritance for classes?
questions.title: Why Java Doesn't Support Multiple Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: Java forbids a class from extending two classes to avoid the **diamond problem**: if two parents provide a method (or field) with the same signature, the compiler can't decide which one the child inherits, creating ambiguity. Java keeps class inheritance single and unambiguous, and lets you achieve multiple inheritance of **type** through **interfaces** instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the diamond problem and that interfaces sidestep it (no instance state to conflict).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Java 'just doesn't allow it' without explaining the diamond ambiguity, or thinking interfaces don't have the same issue.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain interfaces avoid the state conflict, and for clashing default methods the class must override and use InterfaceName.super.method().

sections.title: Why No Multiple Class Inheritance — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Java doesn't let a class `extends` more than one class. The reason is the **diamond problem**: imagine class `D` extending both `B` and `C`, which both extend `A` and both override a method `greet()`. When you call `d.greet()`, which version wins — `B`'s or `C`'s? There's no unambiguous answer, and the problem gets worse with conflicting **fields** and constructor chains.

To keep the language simple and unambiguous, Java allows only **single** inheritance of classes. You still get multiple inheritance of **type** through **interfaces** — a class can implement many — because interfaces historically carried **no state and no implementation**, so there was nothing to conflict.

sections.title: The Diamond Problem
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A["A: greet()"] --> B["B: greet() override"] A --> C["C: greet() override"] B --> D["D extends B and C?"] C --> D D --> Q["d.greet(): B's or C's?
Ambiguous — forbidden"] ```

sections.title: How Interfaces Sidestep It
sections.content:
Interfaces let a class take on many types without the diamond ambiguity.

- Classic interfaces had **only method signatures** — no bodies, no fields — so implementing two couldn't create conflicting state or behavior.
- A class can `implements A, B, C` freely and provides the single implementation itself.
- Java 8 `default` methods reintroduced a mild conflict possibility: if two interfaces give the **same default method**, the class **must override it** and can pick one via `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- There are still no instance fields in interfaces, so the *state* part of the diamond never arises.

sections.title: Multiple Inheritance of Type via Interfaces
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Java just doesn't allow it'**: explain the *why* — the diamond ambiguity over methods, fields, and constructors.
- **Thinking interfaces can't clash**: conflicting `default` methods do clash, but the class must override and resolve.
- **Forgetting state**: the real danger is duplicated/conflicting **fields**, which interfaces avoid by having none.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A class can `extends` only **one** class — to avoid the **diamond problem**.
- Ambiguity arises from conflicting inherited **methods, fields, and constructors**.
- Interfaces give multiple inheritance of **type** (a class implements many).
- Interfaces have **no instance state**, so the state conflict never occurs.
- Clashing `default` methods → override and use `InterfaceName.super.method()`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Java doesn't allow a class to extend more than one class, and the reason has a name — the diamond problem. Picture a class D that tries to extend both B and C, and B and C both extend a common class A, and both of them override the same method, say greet. Now when you call greet on a D object, which version should it inherit, B's or C's? There's no unambiguous answer. And it gets worse than just methods — you'd also have conflicting fields and conflicting constructor chains to resolve. Rather than invent complicated rules to disambiguate all of that, which is exactly what makes multiple inheritance painful in languages that allow it, Java's designers kept class inheritance single and simple: one parent, no ambiguity. But you don't actually lose the ability to be multiple things, because Java gives you multiple inheritance of type through interfaces. A class can implement as many interfaces as it wants. The reason that's safe is that classic interfaces had no instance fields and no method bodies — just signatures — so implementing two of them couldn't create conflicting state or behavior; the class itself supplies the one implementation. Now, Java 8 added default methods, which do have bodies, so a mild version of the conflict can come back: if two interfaces define the same default method, the compiler makes you override it in your class to resolve the clash, and inside that override you can explicitly call one parent's version by writing the interface name dot super dot the method. But crucially, interfaces still can't hold instance state, so the genuinely nasty part of the diamond — duplicated, conflicting fields — simply never happens.

questions.question: How does constructor chaining work with super() in inheritance?
questions.title: Constructor Chaining with super() in Java
questions.direct_answer: When you create a subclass object, the subclass constructor must run the **parent's constructor first** via `super(args)` — the **first statement**. If you don't write it, the compiler inserts an implicit `super()` (the parent's no-arg constructor). This guarantees the parent part of the object is fully initialized before the subclass adds its own state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know super() runs first, the implicit super() insertion, and the failure when the parent has no no-arg constructor.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing an implicit super() is inserted, leading to a confusing compile error when the parent only has a parameterized constructor.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why parent-first ordering exists (subclass code may rely on inherited state) and how to fix the 'no default constructor in superclass' error.

sections.title: Constructor Chaining with super() — Quick Overview
sections.content:
Every subclass constructor begins by invoking a **parent constructor**. If you write `super(args)`, it must be the **first statement**; if you write nothing, the compiler inserts an implicit **`super()`** calling the parent's no-arg constructor.

This enforces **parent-first** initialization up the whole chain: `Object` is initialized first, then each ancestor, then finally the subclass body. The reason is safety — a subclass often relies on inherited fields, so the parent must be ready before the subclass code runs.

A common gotcha: if the parent has **only a parameterized constructor**, the implicit `super()` doesn't exist and you get a compile error — you must call `super(args)` explicitly.

sections.title: super() Chaining at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Parent first|~always|super() runs before subclass body|whole chain top-down|Object initialized first
blue|Implicit super()|~when you omit it|compiler inserts super()|calls parent no-arg ctor|first statement
emerald|Must be first|~the rule|super(args) first statement|or this(...) instead|not both
rose|Common error|~parent has no no-arg ctor|implicit super() fails|'no default constructor'|call super(args) explicitly

sections.title: Compile error — missing explicit super(args)
Fix — call super(args) explicitly first
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing about implicit `super()`**: it's why a missing parent no-arg constructor causes a confusing error.
- **Putting code before `super(...)`**: it must be the first statement.
- **Expecting subclass-first init**: the parent is always initialized before the subclass body.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A subclass constructor calls a parent constructor **first**, via `super(args)` or implicit `super()`.
- The compiler inserts `super()` only if you write neither `super(...)` nor `this(...)`.
- Initialization is **parent-first** up the whole chain (`Object` first).
- If the parent lacks a no-arg constructor, you **must** call `super(args)` explicitly.
- `super(...)` must be the **first statement** of the constructor.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Constructor chaining with super is about how a subclass object gets fully built, and the core rule is that the parent constructor always runs before the subclass constructor's body. Concretely, the first thing a subclass constructor does is call a parent constructor. If you explicitly write super with arguments, that has to be the very first statement. And if you don't write any super call at all, the compiler quietly inserts an implicit call to the parent's no-argument constructor for you. This chains all the way up: when you create a Dog, the constructor for Object runs first, then Animal, then Dog. The reason for this parent-first ordering is safety — a subclass frequently uses fields it inherited from the parent, so the parent part of the object has to be completely initialized before any subclass code runs. Now here's the gotcha that trips up almost every fresher. The implicit super call is specifically a call to the parent's no-arg constructor. So if the parent class only defines a constructor that takes arguments, there is no no-arg constructor for Java to call, and you get a compile error that says something like there's no default constructor available in the superclass. People find that confusing because they didn't write any super call at all — but the compiler tried to, and failed. The fix is simple: in the subclass constructor, explicitly call super with the required arguments as the first statement. So whenever a parent only has a parameterized constructor, you know the subclass must explicitly chain to it.

questions.question: What is the difference between method overriding and method hiding in Java?
questions.title: Method Overriding vs Method Hiding in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Overriding** applies to **instance** methods: the subclass version is chosen at **runtime** by the actual object type (dynamic dispatch). **Method hiding** applies to **static** methods with the same signature: which one runs is decided at **compile time** by the **reference type**, not the object. So overriding is polymorphic; hiding is not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know static methods are hidden (not overridden) and resolved by reference type at compile time.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing a static method can be overridden, expecting polymorphic dispatch when calling a hidden static method through a parent reference.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Demonstrate the difference with a parent reference to a child object: the instance method dispatches to the child, the static method resolves to the parent.

sections.title: Overriding vs Method Hiding — Quick Overview
sections.content:
These look identical in code but behave oppositely. **Overriding** is for **instance** methods: a subclass redefines an inherited instance method with the same signature, and the JVM picks the version based on the **actual object** at **runtime**. That's polymorphism.

**Method hiding** happens with **static** methods: if a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as the parent's, it doesn't override it — it **hides** it. Which one runs is decided at **compile time** by the **type of the reference**, not the object.

So `Parent p = new Child()`: calling an instance method runs `Child`'s (overriding), but calling a static method runs `Parent`'s (hiding).

sections.title: Overriding vs Hiding at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Overriding|~instance methods|chosen at runtime|by actual object type|polymorphic
blue|Method hiding|~static methods|chosen at compile time|by reference type|not polymorphic
emerald|Same code, diff result|~Parent p = new Child()|instance -> Child's|static -> Parent's|the classic gotcha
violet|Guidance|~don't rely on hiding|call static via class name|Parent.method()|avoid confusion

sections.title: Overriding vs Method Hiding
sections.content:
| Aspect | Overriding | Method hiding |
|---|---|---|
| **Method kind** | Instance | Static |
| **Resolved at** | Runtime | Compile time |
| **Based on** | Actual object type | Reference type |
| **Polymorphic?** | Yes | No |
| **`@Override` allowed?** | Yes | No (compile error) |
| **`Parent p = new Child()`** | Runs Child's | Runs Parent's |

sections.title: The gotcha — same setup, opposite results
Run it through a Parent reference
sections.content:
```java
Parent p = new Child();
System.out.println(p.greet());  // "Child.instance"  <- overriding (runtime)
System.out.println(p.who());    // "Parent.static"   <- hiding (compile-time)
// Best practice: call static methods via the class: Parent.who(), Child.who()
```
*The instance call follows the object; the static call follows the reference type.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Static methods can be overridden'**: they can't — they're hidden, resolved by reference type.
- **Putting `@Override` on a static method**: compile error — it isn't overriding.
- **Calling statics through instances**: misleading; always call static methods via the class name.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Overriding** = instance methods, runtime dispatch on the actual object (polymorphic).
- **Hiding** = static methods, compile-time resolution by the reference type (not polymorphic).
- `Parent p = new Child()`: instance call → Child's; static call → Parent's.
- `@Override` is illegal on static methods.
- Call static methods via the **class name** to avoid confusion.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Method overriding and method hiding look identical when you read the code, but they behave in opposite ways, and the difference comes down to instance versus static. Overriding is for instance methods. When a subclass redefines an inherited instance method with the same signature, the JVM decides which version to run at runtime, based on the actual type of the object. That's polymorphism — a parent reference pointing to a child object will run the child's method. Method hiding is what happens with static methods. If a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as one in the parent, it does not override it — it hides it. And the resolution is completely different: it's decided at compile time, based on the type of the reference variable, not the actual object. The classic demonstration is to write Parent p equals new Child, so the reference type is Parent but the object is a Child. Now if you call an instance method that the child overrode, you get the child's version, because instance methods dispatch on the object at runtime. But if you call a static method that the child hid, you get the parent's version, because static resolution uses the reference type, which is Parent. Same exact setup, opposite results. A couple of practical notes: you cannot put the Override annotation on a static method — it's a compile error, because hiding isn't overriding, and that annotation is actually a nice guard against accidentally thinking you overrode something. And the best practice is to never call static methods through an instance reference at all; call them through the class name, like Parent dot who or Child dot who, so it's crystal clear which one runs and you avoid the whole confusion.

questions.question: What is the difference between IS-A and HAS-A relationships in Java?
questions.title: IS-A vs HAS-A Relationship in Java
questions.direct_answer: **IS-A** is **inheritance**: a subtype *is a kind of* its supertype (`Dog IS-A Animal`), implemented with `extends`/`implements`. **HAS-A** is **composition**: an object *contains* another and uses it (`Car HAS-A Engine`), implemented by holding a field and delegating. Run the IS-A test first; if it fails, model it as HAS-A.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can apply the IS-A vs HAS-A test to choose between inheritance and composition.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing an IS-A (inheritance) relationship where HAS-A (composition) is correct, just to reuse code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note composition (HAS-A) is usually the safer default and that 'favor composition over inheritance' follows directly from this test.

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A — Quick Overview
sections.content:
These two phrases are the test you run to decide between inheritance and composition.

**IS-A** is **inheritance**: the relationship where one type *is a kind of* another. `Dog IS-A Animal`, `Circle IS-A Shape`. You implement it with `extends` (classes) or `implements` (interfaces).

**HAS-A** is **composition**: the relationship where one object *contains and uses* another. `Car HAS-A Engine`, `Order HAS-A List of items`. You implement it by holding the other object as a **field** and delegating to it.

The rule: ask 'is X a kind of Y?' If yes, IS-A (inheritance). If it's really 'X has a Y', it's HAS-A (composition) — and that's usually the safer default.

sections.content:

blue|HAS-A|~composition|Car HAS-A Engine|hold a field + delegate|reuse by containment

sections.title: IS-A vs HAS-A
sections.content:
| Aspect | IS-A (Inheritance) | HAS-A (Composition) |
|---|---|---|
| **Meaning** | Is a kind of | Contains / uses |
| **Java** | `extends` / `implements` | Field + delegation |
| **Example** | `Dog extends Animal` | `Car { Engine engine; }` |
| **Coupling** | Tight | Loose |
| **Flexibility** | Fixed at compile time | Swappable at runtime |
| **Default?** | Only when IS-A truly holds | Usually preferred |

sections.title: Forcing IS-A where HAS-A is correct
sections.content:
```java
// A Car is NOT a kind of Engine — IS-A test fails
class Car extends Engine { } // wrong: inherits Engine's whole API
```

sections.title: Model it as HAS-A (composition)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **IS-A / inheritance** only when the subtype is genuinely a kind of the supertype and is substitutable for it (Liskov) — `Circle IS-A Shape`.

Use **HAS-A / composition** when one object simply uses another's capabilities, when you want to swap that part out, or whenever the IS-A test is shaky. Because composition is loosely coupled and more flexible, the widely-taught guidance 'favor composition over inheritance' is really just 'default to HAS-A unless IS-A clearly holds'.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IS-A** = inheritance (`extends`/`implements`); **HAS-A** = composition (field + delegate).
- Run the **IS-A test** first: 'is X a kind of Y?'
- If it's really 'X has a Y', use composition.
- Composition is **loosely coupled** and swappable; inheritance is tight.
- 'Favor composition over inheritance' = default to HAS-A unless IS-A truly holds.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: IS-A and HAS-A are the two relationships you use to decide between inheritance and composition, and they're basically a sentence test. IS-A is inheritance. It describes a type that is a kind of another type — a dog is an animal, a circle is a shape. You implement that with extends for classes or implements for interfaces, and the subtype inherits the supertype's members. HAS-A is composition. It describes an object that contains and uses another object — a car has an engine, an order has a list of items. You implement that by holding the other object as a field and delegating to it. So the test is literally to phrase the relationship as a sentence: is X a kind of Y? If that's true, it's IS-A, use inheritance. But if the honest sentence is X has a Y, then it's HAS-A, and you should use composition. The classic mistake is forcing an IS-A relationship just to reuse some code. A car is not a kind of engine, so making Car extend Engine is wrong — it inherits the engine's entire API and the relationship doesn't make sense. The right model is composition: the car holds an engine field and calls start on it. And the bonus is flexibility — you can swap that engine out for an electric one later without affecting any code that uses the car. This whole thing connects to the famous guideline, favor composition over inheritance. That advice is really just saying: default to HAS-A unless the IS-A relationship clearly and genuinely holds, because composition is loosely coupled and more flexible, while inheritance is tight coupling that's hard to change later.
